title: Opposition Grows Over Who Jesus Is
overview: Jesus clashes with religious leaders over the Sabbath and the source of his power, and then redefines who counts as his family.

parts.label: Grain picked on the Sabbath (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: The law let people pick a little grain by hand from a neighbor's field, but the Pharisees, a strict and respected group of law teachers, treated it as harvest work banned on the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest. Jesus points to David eating bread reserved for priests, to priests working in the temple, and to the prophet Hosea's words that God wants mercy more than sacrifice, then claims that he, the Son of Man (his name for himself), is lord of the Sabbath.

parts.label: Healing and the gentle servant (vv. 9-21)
parts.note: Jesus says anyone would lift a trapped sheep out of a pit on the Sabbath, so doing good for a person is allowed, and he heals a man's disabled hand while his opponents begin plotting his death. As he withdraws and asks people to keep quiet about him, Matthew sees Isaiah's gentle servant, who will not crush the weak (a bruised reed, a barely burning wick) and in whom other nations will hope.

parts.label: God's power or Satan's? (vv. 22-30)
parts.note: When Jesus heals a blind, mute man, the crowd wonders if he could be the Son of David, the promised king, but the Pharisees say he works by the prince of demons (called Beelzebul or Beelzebub, depending on the translation). Jesus answers that Satan would not fight himself, so this is God's Spirit at work and God's kingdom has arrived, like a strong man (usually read as Satan) being tied up so his house can be raided.

parts.label: The sin not forgiven (vv. 31-37)
parts.note: Jesus says every sin can be forgiven, even words against himself, except blasphemy (insulting speech) against the Holy Spirit. Its exact meaning is debated, but it comes right after his opponents called the Spirit's work Satan's (vv. 24, 28), and he goes on to say, calling them vipers, that words show what fills the heart and will be answered for on judgment day.

parts.label: A sign from Jonah (vv. 38-45)
parts.note: Asked for proof, Jesus offers only a sign drawn from the prophet Jonah: as Jonah was three days and three nights in a great fish, the Son of Man will be that long in the heart of the earth, which Christians read as his burial before rising. The people of Nineveh, who listened to Jonah, and the queen who traveled to hear Solomon will shame those who ignore him, and the spirit returning to a swept but empty house is usually read as warning that a cleanup left empty can end worse.

parts.label: Jesus's true family (vv. 46-50)
parts.note: When his mother and brothers ask to speak with him, Jesus points to his followers and says whoever does his Father's will is his brother, sister and mother. Christians differ on who these brothers were: many Protestants see Mary's later sons, while Catholic and Orthodox Christians understand them as close relatives such as cousins or Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage.

disagreement: Christians differ on what blasphemy against the Spirit is: some tie it closely to the act here of calling the Spirit's work in Jesus demonic, while many, including Catholic teaching and much Protestant teaching, describe a deliberate, lasting refusal of God's mercy that cannot be forgiven because it refuses forgiveness itself.
think: When a rule and someone's real need pull in different directions, how do you decide which should give way?
